body:
Seven children encounter an impossible book. Years later, with the book lost and their lives scattered, dreams of ruins on distant worlds draw them back together.
Sleepwalker is a mythic science-fiction graphic novel. Its questions about time, memory and consciousness also find room in an inquiry and in methods of making: reading a passage closely, following what a witness can know, or discovering how a page turn changes a scene.
Harsh Joshi is developing the story and its world. Sleepwalker is a project of RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited (RTEPL).
Reading the Vedic world closely
A familiar figure can enter a different relationship in another account. A passage can resist the meaning a reader hoped to borrow from it. Following those differences opens questions about time, attention, consciousness and devotion.
Read Markandeya’s encounters across adjacent chapters, or follow a sound towards silence. Particular accounts, translations and interpretations give the inquiry its substance.
The Vedic-world inquiry
Making the story into a page
A character must remain recognisable when the view changes. Moving a speech balloon can change who witnessed an event. A page turn can reveal a relationship that no individual image contained.
The creative methods work through these choices in image and sequence and lettering. Generative workflows make alternatives easier to explore; composition, controlled refinement and reading at the intended size give those alternatives a deliberate form.
Creative methods
Different ways into the same questions
The story lets a reader encounter a world before being given an explanation for it. The essays of the Vedic-world inquiry can stay with a passage or a question, while the creative methods examine the decisions that give an encounter its form. Each can be read independently. A traditional account may inform a scene without becoming its script; a method may suggest a technique without becoming a finished page. These crossings are part of how Sleepwalker is taking shape.

notes.body_html:
Following a revision through the bell example

The essay uses a neutral mystery example, not a Sleepwalker scene. To examine a revision, give that example a few additional stipulated facts: the first witness leaves at 12:15, the third arrives at 12:30, and the bell rings once at noon. The first witness hears it; the third learns about it through the later account. The stopped clock is a separate observation, not a reliable timestamp for the ringing.

Moving the event to one o'clock

This edit invalidates the first witness's opportunity to hear the bell under the stated schedule. It also makes direct hearing possible for the third witness, assuming they remain there. The narrative can retain the first witness's account only by making a further choice: change the departure, change the account's source, or make the account mistaken. Each choice leads to a different story.

The revision therefore travels through event → presence → opportunity → knowledge → any action depending on that knowledge. It does not automatically travel through every reference to the clock. That object becomes affected only if a scene has connected it to the changed event.

Moving the account earlier in the narrative

Keep all event times unchanged and show the first witness's account before the stopped clock. Each witness still has the same opportunity to hear or see what happened. The reader, however, now approaches the clock with knowledge of the bell. An apparent timestamp may look suspicious sooner. This revision travels through reveal → reader inference → later surprise or recognition, without changing the world chronology.

Changing a belief

Suppose the second witness interprets the stopped clock as the time of the bell. Correcting that belief need not change the observed face of the clock. It changes whatever inference or action used the reading as a timestamp. A scene that only describes the clock can remain intact; a scene that relies on the mistaken time needs reconsideration.

An ambiguous editorial instruction has become several concrete choices with different consequences. A graph of these stipulated relationships would expose the affected scenes; deciding which revision makes the better story remains the author's work.

Revision Dependency that changes What can remain intact
Ring at 13:00 instead of noon Presence → hearing opportunity → knowledge A clock description with no asserted link to the bell
Show the account before the clock Reader knowledge → inference → later reveal World chronology and witness presence
Correct the second witness's timestamp belief Interpretation → action based on that time The observed clock face and the noon event

Following the particular relation, rather than every mention of the object, keeps a small revision from becoming an indiscriminate rewrite.

body:
The several orders of a story
A story has more than one order. There is the order in which things happen, the order in which its characters understand them, and the order in which the reader finds out. A mystery depends on their difference: an event can be over before anyone understands it, and a reader can suspect something that a character has yet to see. That gap is something I can write with.
The bell rang once
Imagine a bell ringing at noon. One witness hears it, another sees a stopped clock, and a third arrives later. The narrative shows the clock first, introduces the bell later, and only then lets us hear the first witness's account. Moving that account earlier would change the reader's experience without changing when the bell rang; changing a witness's belief might change their next action while leaving the bell untouched. “Move this earlier” might mean moving the event, a memory of it, or its appearance on the page. Each sends me back to different scenes.
Three sequences trace the bell, the witnesses and the reader, contrasting a change to the event with a change to its telling.
The arrows show sequence, not elapsed time or a shared clock.
Suppose the first witness leaves at 12:15. Moving the bell from noon to 13:00 would remove their chance to hear it. Showing their account earlier changes what the reader knows while leaving those event times intact. The Notes follow the scenes each revision would affect and the choices it leaves me.
The clock's face is an observation, not a reliable timestamp for the bell. Its place in the reader's sequence can suggest a connection before the story gives enough information to judge it.
A clue is a relationship, not only an object
The stopped clock might establish a location, suggest a time, or mislead someone who assumes it is running. If I change where it hangs, the witness's opportunity to see it may disappear. If I change when the reader sees it, the opportunity remains but the inference changes. The clue lives in these relations, not only in the inventory of objects. A later scene may depend on the clock having been seen, on a mistaken conclusion about it, or on the reader remembering its face.
Information architecture helps when it makes those dependencies legible. Instead of rewriting every scene that mentions a clock, I can follow the opportunity, belief and action that the revised premise affected. Where a dependency is uncertain, the uncertainty is itself useful: it exposes a creative choice that still needs an answer.
Belief is not the whole state
Continue the bell example. Suppose the late arrival is frightened when the two witnesses meet later, and the first witness offers support without explaining the event. Trust between them might improve while neither person's knowledge of the bell's cause changes. If a model of the story folds trust and confidence about causes into one score, support becomes evidence by accident. Keeping those states distinct allows a person to feel safer with somebody while still doubting their account.
An institution introduces another path. It receives a genuine account of the bell, but without the stopped clock that would have made it doubt the time. Its staff can become more confident and choose the wrong intervention without anybody inventing a false observation. Restoring the clock to the account changes that inference and the decisions based on it. It need not erase the trust that grew between the witnesses, or undo the consequences of the intervention already made. State changes travel through their particular relationships; one correction is not a reset of the world.
The drawings can change too. A remembered scene might lose colour or break into fragments as a witness begins to doubt their interpretation. The bell still rang at noon. Fear might change how the witness is framed without moving the clock. The image needs to let us distinguish whose experience changed and what they are remembering; otherwise a changed palette can look like a changed event.
In a model that keeps them apart, actions leave something behind in people, relationships and institutions. Accounts can be corrected without erasing consequences, and the same occurrence can be encountered in several forms. The rules are choices about a story, not measurements of human psychology. They are useful if they show me a consequence I would otherwise miss.
When a reading changes the invention
A traditional passage can change what I want an invented rule to do. Following a symbol through its transformations may make its fictional role seem too static, or reveal a consequence I had missed. I might revise that role or keep it as an independent invention. The relation is useful because the reading can push back on the work: an earlier image need not dictate what the passage means, and a passage need not dictate the only story I can make.
Following a change through the story
The story model I am developing for Sleepwalker keeps track of its people and objects, their changing states, the order of scenes, transformations and the images through which we encounter them. An altered observation might unsettle a character's next choice, while an illustration might expose a relation that the prose left vague. Following those changes can send the work in a new direction.
I still have to decide what to do with what the model shows me. Eventually the reader encounters none of this machinery, only the space between panels, a remembered object, an account that arrives late. The several orders become worthwhile when their arrangement lets that reader discover the relation for themselves.

notes.body_html:
A finite period beside the unbounded construction

A finite comparison provides a useful step towards the essay's change of scale. It combines a textual period, a calendar convention and a chosen interval. The 4.32 million human years comes from the commentary accompanying Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.18; the 365-day year and seven-second breath are the illustration's choices. The arithmetic can be examined by changing those choices separately.

N=4,320,000×365×24×60×607≈1.9462×1013. N=\frac{4{,}320{,}000\times365\times24\times60\times60}{7}\approx1.9462\times10^{13}.

That is roughly nineteen trillion intervals.

Note

This particular count is finite. The essay's infinite ratio instead uses an unbounded numerator and the same positive seven-second denominator.

Two different changes to a ratio

Let TT be the long duration and tt the chosen short interval. The count is N=T/tN=T/t. Describing both durations in minutes instead of seconds divides both by sixty and leaves NN unchanged. Choosing a fourteen-second interval instead of a seven-second one halves NN. The first operation changes the unit in which the same quantities are written; the second changes the interval being counted. A larger number can therefore come from a smaller counting interval without any enlargement of the long period.

The dependence is exact:

T/kt/k=Tt=N,Tkt=Nk(k>0). \frac{T/k}{t/k}=\frac{T}{t}=N, \qquad \frac{T}{kt}=\frac Nk\quad(k>0).

Changing the illustrative year from 365 to 366 days, while keeping the number of years and the seven-second interval fixed, multiplies the count by 366/365366/365, an increase of about 0.274 percent. This comparison does not decide which calendar a textual scheme requires. It shows that a convention about the long duration and a choice about the short interval enter the count in different places. Neither is a property of a witness's awareness.

A count and a limit

For finite positive TT and tt, NN is finite. The family Tm=mTT_m=mT, with fixed tt and integer mm growing without bound, instead gives Nm=mNN_m=mN, which grows without bound. That is a precise way to express the unbounded premise of Breath of Cosmos. No member of the family needs to be infinite for its counts to grow without bound. The four-yuga period remains a finite textual quantity; it can supply a starting scale without supplying an upper bound for the thought experiment.

The limit establishes the scale relationship. The essay then asks what it would mean for individual experience to belong to a cosmic or collective consciousness. That interpretation goes beyond counting intervals. If it were developed into a probabilistic model of experiences, it would also need to specify which experiences are possible and how they can occur, much as the typing-monkey comparison requires a sampling rule. Keeping that next question visible preserves the reach of the interpretation and the particular result the calculation supplies.

body:
The world inside a breath
A breath gives an immense world somewhere intimate to begin. Attend to its beginning and end, then imagine an entire life passing within it. From inside that life there were mornings, work, waiting and people who mattered. From the other frame, barely a moment. What would let a reader encounter both scales without losing the person inside the smaller one?
This is one of the questions behind Sleepwalker. In Breath of Cosmos, I begin with a breathing pattern as an input to an imagined model of consciousness, then extend the comparison into cosmic time. The argument makes a definite choice: the cosmic duration is unbounded, while the human breath remains a finite, nonzero interval. Its ratio is infinite. Here I want to follow what that construction makes possible for a story and an image.
The interval stays small; the frame keeps opening
Take the essay's illustrative human breath of seven seconds. Let B be the cosmic duration, expressed in seconds. Then the two directions of the comparison are

\lim_{B\to\infty}\frac{B}{7}=\infty,
\qquad
\lim_{B\to\infty}\frac{7}{B}=0.

The human interval has not become zero. Its proportion tends to zero as the other duration grows without bound. This matters to the imaginative movement: a life does not need to disappear for the frame containing it to become immeasurably larger.
The essay uses breath and time as proxies in a thought experiment about consciousness. Its further possibility is a cosmic or collective consciousness containing individual forms of experience. The limit expresses the scale relation; the interpretation asks what it might mean to belong to that whole. A story gives that question a witness. The witness has a particular history, even when the world exceeds the history's familiar terms.
A calendar can lead the imagination towards the opening
Vedic cosmological accounts give the reader several changes of scale to encounter. In the Bhaktivedanta edition of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 3.11.18 gives a four-yuga cycle whose commentary expresses it as 4.32 million human years. 3.11.22 places a thousand such cycles within Brahmā's day, followed by a night of equal duration. 3.11.38 then compares the two halves of Brahmā's life with a moment for the Supreme. A lifetime on one scale becomes a brief interval on another.
Each specified period is finite, however immense it feels beside a human life. The Brahma-saṁhitā, 5.48, supplies the image of the Brahmās' lives within Mahā-Vishnu's breath. Breath of Cosmos takes that image further: suppose there is no final bound to the duration we are comparing with our own.
The notes calculate how many seven-second intervals fit within one of those finite periods. Here I want to stay with the next step. What happens to the world we thought we knew when the frame around it can keep opening?
The place the witness knows
In Markandeya's encounter, the impossible scale arrives through an ordinary recognition. The witness finds a world inside the child's body, then recognises his own hermitage. The familiar remains there after the frame has become impossible. That recognition makes the encounter more unsettling than a succession of larger containers would have been.
I can imagine drawing the change as a series of receding views: a person, a landscape, a world, another world around it. The figure becomes a marker of size. But what if I keep the reader close to the figure? A remembered path could remain recognisable while its surroundings cease to fit the account. A detail that seemed reassuring could become the very thing that makes the new world impossible to dismiss.
The two compositions offer different experiences of the same ambition. One tells the reader how large the world is. The other lets them discover that the world they know has acquired a place within something they cannot yet understand. The second gives the person more to do than demonstrate scale.
What continues between the frames?
A graphic novel can make that discovery happen through sequence. A place first encountered as ordinary can return with a changed relation to the world around it. The reader carries the earlier encounter across the interval between panels. If every detail changes, recognition becomes difficult; if nothing changes, the expansion may never become an encounter at all.
That brings the cosmic question into the craft of keeping something recognisable through a sequence. Which feature must survive? Where should the reader first notice the difference? What can the witness recognise before they can explain it? These are decisions an author can work on without asking the picture to prove a theory of consciousness.
A small experience can be contained within a larger account and still be the experience through which that account becomes available. The breath supplies a rhythm. The construction opens the scale. The witness brings a world into the encounter, and the story has to let us feel what happens when that world is no longer the whole.

A finite period beside the unbounded construction
A finite comparison provides a useful step towards the essay's change of scale. It combines a textual period, a calendar convention and a chosen interval. The 4.32 million human years comes from the commentary accompanying Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.18; the 365-day year and seven-second breath are the illustration's choices. The arithmetic can be examined by changing those choices separately.

N=\frac{4{,}320{,}000\times365\times24\times60\times60}{7}\approx1.9462\times10^{13}.

That is roughly nineteen trillion intervals.
Note
This particular count is finite. The essay's infinite ratio instead uses an unbounded numerator and the same positive seven-second denominator.
Two different changes to a ratio
Let T be the long duration and t the chosen short interval. The count is N=T/t. Describing both durations in minutes instead of seconds divides both by sixty and leaves N unchanged. Choosing a fourteen-second interval instead of a seven-second one halves N. The first operation changes the unit in which the same quantities are written; the second changes the interval being counted. A larger number can therefore come from a smaller counting interval without any enlargement of the long period.
The dependence is exact:

\frac{T/k}{t/k}=\frac{T}{t}=N,
\qquad \frac{T}{kt}=\frac Nk\quad(k>0).

Changing the illustrative year from 365 to 366 days, while keeping the number of years and the seven-second interval fixed, multiplies the count by 366/365, an increase of about 0.274 percent. This comparison does not decide which calendar a textual scheme requires. It shows that a convention about the long duration and a choice about the short interval enter the count in different places. Neither is a property of a witness's awareness.
A count and a limit
For finite positive T and t, N is finite. The family T_m=mT, with fixed t and integer m growing without bound, instead gives N_m=mN, which grows without bound. That is a precise way to express the unbounded premise of Breath of Cosmos. No member of the family needs to be infinite for its counts to grow without bound. The four-yuga period remains a finite textual quantity; it can supply a starting scale without supplying an upper bound for the thought experiment.
The limit establishes the scale relationship. The essay then asks what it would mean for individual experience to belong to a cosmic or collective consciousness. That interpretation goes beyond counting intervals. If it were developed into a probabilistic model of experiences, it would also need to specify which experiences are possible and how they can occur, much as the typing-monkey comparison requires a sampling rule. Keeping that next question visible preserves the reach of the interpretation and the particular result the calculation supplies.

body:
A figure at a threshold can be smaller than the opening and still hold the centre of a composition. Moving the figure, widening the frame or changing the contrast alters that relationship. The useful discovery is more particular than “this looks good”: something in the arrangement makes the image carry an idea.
In Sleepwalker's Home, the closing view puts a red-scarfed figure on the approach to a circular tower. The city has scale, but the small person facing it gives me a way into that scale. An image is a beginning starts with that frame and asks what would need to survive a revision.
Generative tools make variations available quickly. The craft is in recognising the choice worth developing and carrying it into another frame. Pose and expression need to change without erasing identity; a new view needs to belong to the same space. Controlled refinement can preserve selected relationships while leaving others open to invention. The progression from frame to sequence takes that problem into a page someone else can read.
Continuity reaches beyond appearance. An event can happen before a character understands it, and a reader can see its consequence before its cause. Those different orders of a story let a revelation change the significance of an earlier panel without changing what happened there. Even the position of a few words can change whose account the reader receives. Structure makes those relationships workable; composition and pacing give them an experience.
A variation can reveal something worth keeping. Put two good images next to each other, though, and they may tell a story neither told alone. That is where making the page starts to change the idea.

body:
A compelling frame offers a relationship worth keeping: a figure's scale, an opening around it, a line of light. Following it into another image asks which parts can vary while the person and place remain recognisable. Following those images onto a page asks what the reader can infer between them.
That progression changes the unit of the work. The individual image becomes a continuous presence, then a sequence whose meaning exceeds any one frame. What began as a visual choice becomes an experience someone else completes.

body:
An image is a beginning
A generated frame can show me something I did not know how to ask for. That is part of its appeal: the image arrives before the intention is fully verbal, and choosing what to keep can become a way of discovering the intention. Carrying the discovery into another frame asks a harder question. What, exactly, was worth keeping?
The part that mattered
A small figure before an enormous threshold can hold the relationship I want even when its materials are wrong. Another image can have exquisite surfaces and lose the relationship entirely. If I judge both by how impressive they look in isolation, I have no reliable way to choose between them.
Sleepwalker's visual direction begins with the human anchor. The environment carries scale, but the person gives that scale a reason to be felt. A cool field and warm focal light can guide attention towards that relation; weathered surfaces can make the environment feel like something encountered rather than freshly invented. A return path or an object someone has maintained can suggest a world inhabited beyond its spectacle. Those treatments work when the composition already holds the person and the threshold together. The prompt becomes a way to discover which decision should survive the next attempt, rather than a request to produce the whole work at once.
A red-scarfed figure stands on a stone forecourt, facing a distant circular tower across water channels; the dark figure interrupts the warm central axis of the city.
The closing composition from Sleepwalker's Home.
The figure stands directly on the approach to the circular tower. Its dark silhouette interrupts the warm central line, while the scarf gives the nearby body a small movement against the enormous, nearly symmetrical setting. The city could remain impressive without the figure; with it, the image asks where someone is standing and what they are facing. That is a relation I can point to and try to preserve.
One prompt cannot hold every decision equally
Composition, character identity, expression, environment and lettering are different kinds of work. Asking one generation to solve them together makes it difficult to improve one without disturbing the others. The route I intend to explore begins with frames I direct in Midjourney, followed by local ComfyUI and controlled refinement that separates those decisions. A composition can remain fixed while a character's treatment changes; a pose can be specified separately from the appearance of the person holding it. Lettering can be composed for the page rather than left to chance in an image.
Separating those decisions lets each change become more legible. If a revised pose turns inquiry into confrontation, I can see what the pose did without also changing the environment. If the colour treatment moves the emotional centre, I can reconsider that treatment while retaining the staging. Controlled work makes room for discovery because fewer unrelated choices are lost with each attempt.
Making a change without losing the frame
A workable study can start in the least polished form: a thumbnail fixing the small figure, the opening and the masses beyond it. At that scale, a stronger silhouette can do more than a more intricate building. I would carry the chosen composition into a pose or depth condition, develop the person's identity separately, and then work on the environment around the person. Masks make the separation practical: an expression can change inside one region while the important contour and light direction outside it remain deliberate choices.
Spatial conditioning is useful here because it holds a different sort of information from a text prompt. The ControlNet paper develops conditions including edges, depth and human pose. A depth map can help preserve the threshold's spatial relation while a pose condition gives the person a specific action. Neither names the emotional proposition of the scene. That remains in the staging: whether the shoulders yield, whether the head looks into the space, and how much distance the composition leaves before entry.
Environment, lettering and final paint-over then answer their own questions. A ruin can carry mass and silence without an indiscriminate layer of luminous glyphs. Lettering needs space before the surface detail fills the page. Paint-over can recover a hand, a face or a material boundary that the generation made plausible but narratively wrong. These are not failures to automate enough. They are places where the work needs a decision finer than “make another image”.
For the threshold study, the stages would carry different decisions forward:
Stage	Decision worth retaining	What can still change	
Thumbnail	Small figure, opening and large surrounding masses	Materials, detail and expression	
Spatial conditioning	Pose and depth relationship	Surface treatment within that geometry	
Character and environment passes	Recognisable person and the light connecting them to the threshold	Local corrections inside selected masks	
Lettering and paint-over	Reading order, gesture and emotional focus	Detail that competes with the sequence	
Keeping the conditioning inputs and model choices makes an attempt repeatable enough to investigate, but the thumbnail remains an important check against false progress. A beautiful render that hides the witness behind ornament has lost the composition's point. A rougher one that preserves the relation may be the better foundation. The sequence must retain the decision the frame helped me discover.
The image can disagree with the idea
A drawing may reveal that a scene's supposed emotional centre is somewhere else, or expose a weakness in the written premise. I want that disagreement to be possible: the image can send a question back to the work, and I can choose whether to follow it. The same openness matters in reading a tradition, where a source can resist what I hoped to make from it. When a frame does reveal a compelling relation, keeping the character through a small sequence lets me follow how that relation changes. What survives is a choice I can understand and develop, rather than a look I can only try to repeat.

A small continuity study

An invented three-panel doorway sequence offers a small study of recognisability. Varying the view and then the material treatment would separate two ways a sequence can lose the person it is meant to follow.

Separating a change of view from a change of person

One proposed comparison holds the room layout and clothing design fixed while the person notices the doorway, approaches it and turns back. Pose and viewpoint vary. The question is whether the silhouette, proportions, clothing and placement of a carried object keep the person recognisable through those changes. Copying one face into all three views would evade part of the problem rather than solve it.

A second comparison keeps the intended action and staging but changes the material register, for example from a lived view to recovered memory. This asks whether recognition survives the treatment change. If the first comparison already fails, the second cannot tell us whether the material change caused the loss. Establishing ordinary continuity first makes the expressive variation easier to interpret.

Zhang, Rao and Agrawala's ControlNet paper supplies spatial-conditioning techniques, including edges, depth, segmentation and pose. A workflow record would explain which inputs produced an attempt. Recognition belongs to the resulting sequence: matching settings cannot substitute for a person remaining legible through the turn.

Three scales of inspection

Viewing scale What can remain clear What can disappear
Thumbnail Movement, doorway and turn Small identity details
Lettered page Gesture and speaker order An action covered by a balloon
Intended reading size The features carrying recognition or a clue Fine distinctions visible only at production resolution

Tip

Compare the sequence at all three viewing scales. A frame can succeed at one scale and fail at another. The point of comparing them is to find where the reading breaks, not to give every render an identical checklist score.

The comparisons separate identity, staging and treatment sufficiently to make a failed sequence informative about the next revision.

body:
Keeping a character through a sequence
The reader sees a change before they know why it happened. In a comic, that is powerful. In generated art, it can also be an accident. If the face, clothing or position of a carried object changes between two panels, the reader may take it as an event. A production inconsistency has acquired narrative meaning before anyone intended it to.
An early extraction for Sleepwalker's website made this problem concrete. The request was to separate a standing figure from its forest background. In the source, the figure's chest faced the viewer, with the head turned slightly to one side; the first extraction showed the figure's back. A change meant to remove scenery had changed the encounter: facing the reader and turning away invite different readings of attention and intention. The corrective request specified the original facing direction, shoulder position, lowered hands, proportions, clothing and bare feet. It asked for the person to remain the same while the background disappeared. The important constraint was the relation the pose carried, not simply a recognisable face.
Recognition has more than one input
Consider a neutral sequence: a person notices a doorway, approaches it and turns back. Expression and pose change. The silhouette, proportions and clothing need enough continuity for the person to remain recognisable. The doorway moves within the frame as the viewpoint changes, but its relation to the room must still make sense.
A continuity sheet describes the person across views; a pose guide describes the action; a composition sketch describes where that action sits. A seed records one generation input rather than defining any of these relationships. The ControlNet paper describes spatial conditioning through inputs such as edges, depth and pose, giving the process a way to hold some spatial relations more deliberately. Character recognition still depends on which features remain legible through the changed view, and narrative meaning depends on what the sequence does with them.
A different image can still be the same event
Sleepwalker's visual direction allows the same event to change with viewpoint, memory or emotional state. A recovered memory can have a different material treatment from a lived event while retaining the person, room and significant gesture. Recognition carries the relation across the change; the altered treatment lets the reader experience another way of approaching it.
The stable relation gives the variation something to disturb. A repeated composition with one changed detail can focus attention on that detail. If every feature changes at once, the reader may lose the very connection through which the variation was meant to speak. Continuity therefore creates expressive range rather than requiring every frame to look identical.
The register changes for a reason
The doorway study can move through several visual registers without changing its event. In a lived view, clear silhouettes and a cool illuminated field keep the person near. In recovered memory, amber and worn print can change the material distance while retaining the doorway and the gesture. A dream might begin with those same particulars and break only one relation: the opening grows beyond the wall that contains it, while the hand and the room remain recognisable. The impossible scale becomes legible because the rest of the image continues to honour the ordinary setting.
That single break is more useful than unrestricted surrealism. If the face, room, pose and viewpoint all drift, the reader cannot locate what became impossible. A maskable transformation also gives production a tractable question: preserve the agreed identity and geometry, then apply the intended break to the chosen relation. Dream logic has become a compositional operation rather than a prompt for strangeness.
For a study in corrupted attribution, I could repeat two nearly symmetric panels and alter just a shadow or the direction of a speech-balloon tail. The observation remains familiar while the reader's account of who acted becomes uncertain. The altered detail has to survive the intended viewing size; a clue that only exists at production resolution cannot do the same work on a phone. The change gives uncertainty a visible location in an otherwise familiar composition.
Resolution need not erase the difference. Two viewpoints could retain distinct palettes on one spread while their shared spatial relation finally aligns. The views become intelligible together, not interchangeable. In that possibility, continuity preserves both recognition and plurality: the same encounter can be followed through more than one way of seeing it.
Register	Relation retained	Deliberate variation	
Lived event	Person, doorway and action	Clear silhouettes in a cool illuminated field	
Recovered memory	Recognisable place and gesture	Amber, worn-print material distance	
Dream	Hand and ordinary room	Opening grows beyond its containing wall	
Corrupted attribution	Familiar observation	A shadow or balloon tail changes who seems responsible	
Resolution	Shared spatial relation	Distinct viewpoints align without losing their palettes	
The record explains an attempt, not its meaning
Keeping the workflow, models, conditioning inputs and parameters makes a changed result easier to inspect. Judging the sequence requires another scale of attention. A consistent face may draw attention away from the action; a speech balloon may cover the gesture that connects two panels; a page legible at full size may lose the relation on a phone. The production record explains an attempt, while thumbnails, lettering and the intended viewing size expose what that attempt lets a reader see.
Recognition lets a change become meaningful: the reader sees that this is the person they knew, now turning away, returning or noticing something. Between the panels, they supply what the images leave out. Continuity gives that participation a stable world to act upon.

body:
What happens between the panels
A hand approaches a closed door. In the next panel, a person stands inside the room. The door opened somewhere between the images, although nobody drew it opening. The reader made that part of the story happen, connecting the two visible moments with an action the page left out.
Change the second panel to the person still outside, facing a locked door, and the relationship changes. Add somebody else holding a key and another explanation becomes possible. The images do not need a caption announcing each inference. Their arrangement gives the reader something to do.
A person reaches towards a closed door; in the next panel, that person stands inside the room.
A: the next frame supplies a consequence. Outside → inside.
A person reaches towards a closed door; in the next panel, they remain outside beside another person holding a key.
B: the next frame opens another possibility. Outside → outside, with someone holding a key.
The first frame is the same. The different second frames invite different accounts of the action left between them.
The strongest image may be wrong for the page
A beautiful establishing frame can be redundant if the previous panel has already established the place. A spectacular interior can expose what a later page needs to withhold. A panel belongs to an action, a rhythm and an order of discovery: it may introduce the situation, sustain an unresolved moment, carry its turn or leave room for the consequence. A quieter frame can do more for the page if it lets the reader recognise what has changed.
The missing action belongs to the mystery
A later revelation can revise the explanation of what the reader saw without replacing the observation. The door was closed; perhaps someone else opened it. The first explanation was incomplete, not necessarily the image. That possibility depends on ordinary continuity. If a handle changes sides because generation drifted, it may look like a clue; repeated accidents make it hard to know which discrepancies deserve attention. Keeping continuity through a sequence gives the reader a baseline against which an intentional discrepancy can matter.
Attention changes the interval
A sequence can sustain the doorway without repeatedly establishing it. One panel gives the place, another the hand approaching, a narrow interval holds the hesitation, and the next carries the irreversible discovery. A release panel can then show what the discovery did to the person. Changing the space given to hesitation changes how long the reader inhabits it, even when the imagined event lasts no longer. Moment-to-moment transitions attend to small changes; aspect-to-aspect views can gather a place through several details before its full relation becomes apparent.
Words also take time to cross a page. A line can reach us before its speaker appears, carrying a voice through the interval. Where that voice belongs depends on the lettering and the space around it, another part of the composition rather than a caption explaining what the images already show.
The page has a body
A reveal placed after a page turn arrives differently from the same reveal visible on the current spread. A phone's scroll is another physical arrangement: the words and images may be unchanged while the timing is not. I am interested in that material part of reading, the distance between frames, the density of a page, the room a silence receives. A dream sequence can alter one of those relations and let the disturbance travel through an otherwise recognisable page.
What the page leaves out can become part of what it expresses. The event, the character's account and the reader's discovery meet in that space, with the reader supplying a relation rather than receiving its explanation. The door can stay unchanged on the page while becoming a different door in the reader's memory.
Scott McCloud's Understanding Comics (1993) calls the space between panels the gutter and the reader's work across it closure; moment-to-moment and aspect-to-aspect are two of the six transitions he names. The release panel is one of Neil Cohn's narrative categories in The Visual Language of Comics (2013).

body:
Words and the space around them
Put “I saw it” beside two figures. A balloon pointing to the nearer figure makes one person the witness; a tail reaching towards the other changes who claims to have seen. Put the words in an established memory caption instead, and the moment of speaking may lie elsewhere. The sentence has not changed. Its place on the page has changed the account it gives us.
That makes lettering part of the story's evidence. If a later panel reveals that the apparent speaker was repeating somebody else's account, the first arrangement must have left room for that discovery. An arbitrary tail or a decorative change of type would spend the reader's attention on a relation the story never meant to offer. Ambiguity can be deliberate, but it needs a relationship worth being uncertain about.
A voice reaches the page
A line of speech can reach across a boundary before its speaker is visible. The reader encounters a voice, then discovers where it came from. Detached text can suggest another register only if its typography and position give a reason to read it differently. I want that difference to survive beyond colour: a person's speech, a machine translation and a remembered voice should remain distinguishable through shape, spacing and consistent conventions.
The convention earns trust through ordinary use. Once a reader knows how a remembered voice looks, a departure can become consequential. If every line arrives in a newly invented treatment, the departure has no baseline. The page asks the reader to learn a new code each time instead of following what the voice says.
Lettering also makes a route through a panel. Two balloons can be legible separately and still leave their order uncertain. Moving a line to make room for an image can change who seems to answer whom. I would review the exchange at the size it will actually be read, including a phone: the words, their order and their relation to the figures need to hold together. Enlarging a beautiful frame does not repair an exchange that cannot be followed.
A mark can extend beyond its pieces
Negative space can hold an unfinished relation rather than merely make a page elegant. Consider fragments of an invented glyph placed in successive panels. Their alignment could leave a shape in the space between them that no individual panel contains. Moving the fragments would alter that shape without changing the fragments themselves. This is one way an invented script could carry meaning in an arrangement, not only in its separate marks.
The gap needs to do something visible. If the pieces form the same complete mark inside each panel, their repetition only decorates the sequence. body:
What does Markandeya recognise inside a world contained by a child, and after that impossible encounter, what does he ask for? The passage turns somewhere between the two. I want to follow that turn, including the part that a retelling centred on cosmic spectacle might leave behind.

body:
Following a symbol through its transformations
A sound grows quieter, and attention grows more absorbed. That movement interests me more than a symbol made louder until its meaning is impossible to miss. In the nāda passages of the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā, what attention follows changes as the account develops. Reading the movement gives me something a dictionary entry cannot: a relation between a form, the attention it gathers and what happens when the form no longer holds the foreground.
A sound followed into silence
I am reading Svātmārāma through Pancham Sinh's 1914 English translation. In chapter IV, Sanskrit-numbered verses 84–86 move from loud, varied sounds through drums and bells towards finer comparisons such as flute, vīṇā and bee. Later, Sanskrit-numbered 101–102 associate the disappearance of sound with the supreme culmination and distinguish heard nāda as Shakti from formless Parameshvara. These are movements within the text's yogic and theological account, not an acoustic mechanism.
The middle of the account complicates a simple fading sound. Sanskrit-numbered verses 87–89 describe attention to subtler sound even amid loud sound, movement between coarse and subtle, and steadiness where the mind first attaches. The sequence is about the relation of attention to its object, not only the object's decreasing intensity. Verse 90 then compares absorption to a bee intent on nectar rather than the flower's scent. Several images carry a changing relation; no isolated label gives me that movement.
That is what interests me beyond a one-word definition of anāhata. A form can gather attention without remaining its loudest object. In a drawing, a repeated mark might prepare the reader to notice an interval after the mark disappears. That is a creative response to the reading: the composition could carry a consequence that a larger sacred emblem would merely announce.
When the sound stops
A story can make knowledge actionable through a changed relationship. A person might already know the relevant fact but be unable to act on it until trust, attention or their relation to another witness changes. That gives the reading a narrative question to work on without assigning a fixed fictional meaning to the text's symbol.
Consider a neutral compositional study rather than a proposed scene. Two people have learnt to listen for the same tone, yet each has treated the other as an unreliable witness. The tone stops. What matters now is whether they can recognise each other's attention without the external cue that previously organised it. One might act, the other might refuse, and either choice can change their trust. Silence has acquired a consequence. Drawing a glowing symbol between them would be weaker if it supplied only an announcement that something sacred happened.
The visual work could preserve that consequence through position, interval and negative space. A repeated alignment can remain after its central mark has disappeared. The reader sees that a relation persists although the object used to announce it no longer does. A symbol's transformation has become something the composition can carry, rather than a definition it must display.
Meaning moves with the encounter
A symbol's function depends on its neighbours, on who meets it and on what the encounter changes. The Markandeya passages make the heart a setting for a divine arrival (12.10.10); the yoga passage follows inward sound towards absorption. Shared language can invite a comparison without establishing identical experiences or doctrines. The difference between their movements is part of their substance.
An invented relation can then change what someone believes, how they act and what the reader encounters. Those orders of a story give the symbol room to work over time. Its significance may emerge through a gesture recognised later, or through trust altered by a silence. The meaning belongs to the encounter, not to a label detached from everything that happens around it.
In the chapter IV text, the English paragraphs are numbered one lower than the Sanskrit verses cited here: 84–86 correspond to 83–85, 87–89 to 86–88, 90 to 89, and 101–102 to 100–101.

body:
An immense revelation can seem like the end of a story. In the Bhāgavata, Markandeya's encounter with the cosmic child continues into another meeting, another setting and a request. Reading the adjacent chapters together lets the later response change what the earlier spectacle means.
The first article stays with the immense world, and the second follows what the witness does next. The order matters because seeing more does not settle what the witness wants, or how he relates to what he has seen.
The encounter also leaves me with a question about description: what happens when the world no longer fits the terms in which a witness understood it? Causality takes up that question in mathematical terms, asking which distinctions a description can express and when it needs to change. Here I am reading a theological encounter, with its own meaning and ending; the question can travel without turning the encounter into a mathematical claim.

notes.body_html:
The order of recognition

Note

The reading follows one particular edition. It uses the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust's English rendering of the twelfth canto of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

12.9.27 supplies the inhalation and the witness's bewilderment. 12.9.28–29 elaborates the recognised world and its temporal divisions. 12.9.30 supplies the recognition of his own hermitage and the return with the exhalation.

Containment and encounter are different orders

A containment sketch could put the world inside the child and the witness inside that world. It would describe a spatial relationship but omit the order in which Markandeya encounters it. The passage supplies a succession: entry, an elaborated world, recognition of his own hermitage, then return. The listed occupations and divisions of time give that world ongoing activity, not only nested scenery.

Imagine two visual responses to that succession. The first begins with the whole arrangement visible, including the hermitage. Later panels draw closer to the witness. The reader knows where he is before he does; his recognition becomes an experience the reader watches him reach. The second begins at entry, follows rivers and inhabited places, and delays the familiar hermitage. Here the reader can share the discovery rather than wait for the witness to catch up. Both responses could retain the same spatial arrangement and finish at the same return. What changes is the relationship between the witness's knowledge and the reader's.

The second response still needs more than a caption saying “his hermitage”. A recurring contour, arrangement or object could make the place recognisable before it is named. If that recognition depends on visual information never given to the reader, the caption supplies an explanation but the image cannot supply the encounter. The compositional question is which familiar detail can survive the new scale long enough to be recognised.

Visual form What it makes available immediately What it can withhold
Nested containment diagram Child, world and witness as simultaneous relations Little of the sequence of discovery
Ordered panels Entry, encounter and return as successive experiences The hermitage until recognition becomes consequential

Giving the reader information earlier is not necessarily a lesser choice. It can make the witness's hesitation, disbelief or eventual recognition the centre of attention. Withholding it instead puts discovery at the centre. The arrangement earns its form through the encounter it makes possible, not through a contest over which picture is more cosmically accurate.

body:
Markandeya and the size of a world
The detail that holds my attention is not just the size of the universe. It is that the familiar world is still there. In the Bhaktivedanta rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 12.9.27, Markandeya is drawn into the child's body with an inhalation. What he encounters inside is a world he recognises. The narrative turns what seemed to contain everything into something contained, then lets recognition complicate the impossible change of scale.
The ordinary survives the extraordinary
The following verses, 12.9.28–29, do not remain at the level of abstract cosmic grandeur. The account includes rivers, settlements, occupations and the divisions of time. In 12.9.30, the witness recognises his own hermitage before the child's exhalation returns him to the waters.
That movement changes the frame without making the particulars irrelevant. Rivers, work and the divisions of time give the witness more than an abstract universe to contemplate. Recognition reaches as far as his own hermitage, something intimate within the immense account. My reading is that an altered perspective can make familiar life strange without making it disposable. The encounter's force comes through the persistence of particulars in a place where the witness did not expect them.
The witness gives the scale somewhere to land
A diagram can show one container inside another. A narrative gives the change to someone who has to undergo it. Recognition, bewilderment and the return to a previous frame make cosmic scale a sequence of experiences. I can follow the encounter through a witness who cannot immediately reconcile what he sees, even when I cannot reconcile the frames myself. That is part of what draws me towards Markandeya in Sleepwalker's wider inquiry: his limits matter alongside what he witnesses. A world vast enough to disorient him still contains a place he knows, holding bewilderment and recognition together.
An image could preserve the relationship
A visual response might hold one ordinary detail through a radical change of scale: a river, a place, a recognisable human silhouette. The large world needs the small witness, and the witness needs something recognisable within the large world. Keeping that relationship in the composition could make scale felt through the particulars that survive it.
I would delay the hermitage rather than place it in the opening diagram. First the reader encounters the unexpected world; only then does a small familiar shape bring it close. The visual sequence can let recognition happen, instead of labelling a nested universe before the witness has found his place in it.
A familiar rhythm and a familiar place can each give an immense frame a point of contact. The breath supplies an interval we can experience; the hermitage supplies a place the witness recognises. Neither small thing merely demonstrates how large the frame has become. Each preserves a point from which that frame can be experienced.

body:
What the witness asks for
What would I ask for after seeing a world inside a child? Greater sight, perhaps, or an explanation of how the familiar hermitage could exist in that impossible setting. Markandeya's next encounter takes the question elsewhere. The witness has seen something immense; what he asks to keep is a relationship.
What follows the extraordinary encounter?
The familiar image of Markandeya inside a child's breath can end with cosmic amazement. The Bhāgavata continues. After the encounter, 12.10.2 gives the sage a prayer in which māyā can appear in the guise of knowledge and bewilder even divine beings. In the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust translation, he responds by taking shelter in Hari. The narrative's answer is devotional, not a better diagram of the universe. That changes the question I bring back to the encounter: what does seeing something immense do to the witness's confidence in what he knows?
A spectacular revelation often gives a fictional character new explanatory power. Here I find another possibility. The experience can alter the relation to explanation itself. If apparent knowledge can participate in bewilderment, another impressive account need not resolve the difficulty. That is my reading of the narrative turn, rather than an argument that studying the world is futile. The text's devotional response and my question about confidence meet without becoming the same statement.
The heart is another setting
The next encounter moves inward. In 12.10.9, Markandeya's absorption is so complete that he does not notice Shiva and Uma arriving. 12.10.10 describes Shiva entering the hidden space of his heart, comparing the entrance to air passing through an opening. The cosmographic witness is now the site of an encounter he did not perceive externally. The narrative can make an enormous world intimate without shrinking its significance.
What attracts me is the movement between settings. The sage recognises his hermitage inside the cosmic child; later a divine visitor enters the sage's interior. A simple inside-and-outside diagram cannot carry the whole relation, because whose interior it is and how the encounter happens both change. The text makes the reader follow a person through those changes. That attention to encounter is richer than assigning each figure one permanent function.
When a boon is offered, 12.10.34 has Markandeya ask for unwavering devotion to the Lord, the Lord's devotees and Shiva. The BBT commentary explicitly interprets Shiva's place through its Vaishnava theology. That interpretive setting matters. It is not a neutral legend in which familiar names can be freely substituted, nor a statement that every tradition arranges their relationships this way.
The sequence has moved twice: from the witness seeing an immense world to a visitor entering the witness, then from extraordinary perception to a request about devotion. The boon does not merely reward how much he has seen. It concerns the relation he wishes to keep. That makes the final request an essential part of my reading, rather than an epilogue after the interesting cosmic scene.
Recognition does not make every account one biography
The short-life Markandeya, the encounter with death and Shiva, and the witness to dissolution invite comparison. They should not be joined merely because the name is familiar. Even within these two adjacent Bhāgavata chapters, a close reading discovers different relations: witness and world, knowledge and bewilderment, inner absorption and external arrival, gift and devotion. A comparison with another text needs the particular account it contributes, not a generic “Markandeya story” assembled from memory.
This is where the inquiry becomes personally useful. I begin with a name I recognise, follow a passage until it changes the question, and return to the name with less certainty but more substance. The world inside the child remains immense, but its witness no longer appears only as someone who saw it. His absorption and the devotion he requests give the encounter a life beyond its spectacle. Sometimes that reading changes the fiction. Sometimes it changes only the reader. Both are reasons to continue.

Privacy notice
RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited (RTEPL) is responsible for deciding how personal data is used on rawthoughts.in, causality.in, sleepwalker.in and post-agi-economics.org, and on their subdomains, including the documentation at docs.rawthoughts.in and docs.causality.in. RTEPL publishes and operates these websites. This notice explains the information handled when you read these websites or use their contact and reading tools.
Visiting the website
GitHub Pages hosts these publications. Serving a page involves connection information, including your IP address and the page requested. GitHub logs visitors’ IP addresses for security, including when a visitor is not signed in. GitHub handles that information under its privacy statement and may process it outside India.
Mintlify hosts the documentation at docs.rawthoughts.in and docs.causality.in. Serving those pages involves the same connection information, which Mintlify handles under its privacy policy and may process outside India. Mintlify's own visitor telemetry is turned off for these sites. Mintlify also provides those two sites' search, page tools and display settings, under the same privacy policy; the in-browser search, assistant tools, display settings and passage links described below belong to the other websites.
On the other websites, search runs in your browser against each website's own index, so what you type is not sent to a search service. Your search is kept in the search page's address, so like any address it can reach GitHub with a page request, appear in your browser history and go with the address if you share it.
If your browser has an assistant that supports it, each page offers that assistant two read-only tools: the text of the page you are reading and the same in-browser search. They work on what the page already shows and send nothing to us; what the assistant does with what it reads follows its provider's terms.
Contacting us
A contact link opens a new message in your own email application. The website does not receive or store the message as a form submission. If you choose to send it, your email service and the recipient's mail service handle the correspondence. Any professional work that follows has its own correspondence and agreement.
For privacy questions, a grievance or a request concerning your personal data, write to info@rtepl.co.in. Include enough information to identify the request, but do not send passwords or unnecessary identity documents. We respond within 30 days and may ask for proportionate verification before disclosing or changing personal data.
Reading preferences
The display settings remember your colour and motion choices in your browser on this device. You can change them in Settings or clear the website's stored data through your browser. These preferences are used to display the page; they stay in your browser and are not sent to us.
After a page loads, your browser may request a few linked pages from the same site and keep copies on this device. These are ordinary page requests to the site's host. The browser can discard the copies, and clearing the site's stored data removes them.
Asking about a passage
When you select text and choose a reading assistant, the link opens that provider with the selected passage, nearby context, the section and article titles, the publication's name, and the article and publication addresses. The passage is limited to 4,096 characters and the nearby context to 1,024. Selecting text alone prepares the link in your browser; choosing the provider sends it there.
The assistant is an external service. The request is included in its link, so it can also appear in your browser history. The provider's own terms, privacy policy and your account settings govern what it does with the request and any conversation that follows. Reading the article does not require using an assistant.
How long information is kept
We keep no record of visits on our own systems; GitHub and Mintlify keep their connection logs for the periods their policies set. Correspondence you send is kept for as long as the matter it concerns needs it and as the law requires.
Security and incidents
These websites hold no accounts and receive no form submissions. If a personal-data breach affects you, we inform you and the authorities as applicable law requires.
Your choices
Following another external link takes you to that service under its own data practices.
You may ask us about your data, request correction or deletion, withdraw consent or raise a concern using the contact above. Requests are handled under applicable law; information needed to comply with a legal obligation or resolve a dispute may need to be kept. Withdrawing consent does not undo processing that has already occurred lawfully.
Changes to the website's data practices will be reflected in this notice. A new optional use that requires consent will ask for that consent rather than treating continued reading as agreement.
